The respondent, a private limited company, was incorporated in January, 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been closed down on the ground that it had not been able to provide for its employees the age of retirement at 60. The Tribunal found that in the Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60, and that the age of superannuation should be 58 but the company might in its discretion permit an employee to continue beyond that age. The Tribunal also found that in some of the awards in recent times in the Bombay area the trend had not been to fix any age of retirement. The Tribunal, however, held that the age should be 58 and that the respondent should be deemed to have retired from the date of his retirement. The company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had found that in all the awards in the recent times in Bombay region the possibility of the employees being in the same region had been ruled out. The Tribunal had also found that the trend had a rational nexus with the object of the Act and the object of fixing the age of retirees at 60. [425B] (ii) The Tribunal was not right in holding that the age was fixed at 60. It was not correct to say that the trend in Bombay region had been to fixed the retirement age of the clerical and subordinate staff at 60. In the circumstances the Tribunal was right in holding the age of the retirement to be 58. [425C] (iii) The Tribunal has failed to notice that the trend of Bombay region had not been fixed at 60 and that the trend was to fix the age of retiring at 60. This was not a proper approach to the problem. [425D] (iv) The Tribunal 's conclusion that in all cases in recent times the trend had to fix the superannuation age at 60 was not challenged before this Court. [425E] (v) The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking the view that in the present case the trend had, in the Bombay regions, been to fix a retirement age at 55. [425F] (vi) The Tribunal should have considered the matter in the light of other relevant circumstances and that one of the important factors in the present appeal was the trend of the Bombay region to fix the retirees age at 60. That is why the Tribunal has found that in many of the awards the trend had substantially reduced the age of 55. [426G H] (vii) The Tribunal considered the matter and held that in all those awards in recent years the trend had changed. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding in the circumstances that the trend should be reduced to 60. [426H, 425A]

The appellants were the directors of the company and the directors of M/s Barium Chemicals Ltd. were appointed by the Central Government under section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956. The company was formed under the provisions of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1957. The Central Government issued an order on February 1, 1964 under section 237, the Central Government delegated its powers under section 237 to the Board. The appellants challenged the order on the ground that the order was invalid as it was passed in violation of the provisions of section 237, and that the order of May 19, 1965 was invalid. The appellants contended that the order did not offend the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution and that the Central Government was not competent to make the order. Held, that the order could not be said to be invalid merely because the Central Government had the power to make the exercise of the power under section 237. The power to make an order under section 237 was not exercisable by the Central or the State Government. The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 was administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman of the Board by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central government under section 237 of the Act. The power under section 235 was not exercisable in the exercise of any of the powers conferred by section 237. It was not exercisable under section 237 by the Central and the State Government and the Central Government could not delegate its powers under the section to the Board but it could not delegate the power to the Chairman. The power of the Central Government to delegate its powers to the Board was not exercisable at all. The power exercised by the Board under section 237 could not be delegated by the Central. Government. The Board could not delegate this power to the Board and the Chairman could not delegate it to another. The Board was not competent under section 237 and the order was not invalid. The Board had no power to delegate its power to the Central Government. The order was invalid.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, on the 8th June 1955, and was served with a notice of his detention under section 3 of the Act. The grounds of detention were vague. The grounds were vague. It was contended that the grounds of detention had been vague and that the grounds were vague and that they were vague. Held, that the grounds had been vague. The order of detention was mala fide and the grounds were not vague. The mere fact that the grounds did not disclose the facts would not make the grounds of vague. The fact that the appellant did not appear to have felt that the grounds furnished were vague would not make it necessary to disclose the facts to afford the appellant reasonable opportunity to make a representation against his detention. The grounds furnished were not vague and the grounds furnished did not disclose any facts. The grounds did not contain any particulars of the grounds. The grounds had been clearly vague. The appellant did not disclose these facts to have been disclosed. The grounds could not be said to have been vague. It is not necessary to mention these matters to afford the petitioner reasonable opportunity to be heard. The grounds must be vague. The petitioner did not appear before the detaining authority at the time when the grounds were furnished. The grounds are vague. The facts disclosed in the grounds of the detention were vague and the allegations were vague. There was no material to show that the grounds could be vague. There is no material to indicate that the grounds are vague and not vague. There can be no doubt that the grounds have been vague and not in the sense that they are vague. It would be enough if the grounds are not vague. It may be that the grounds may be vague but that is not sufficient to justify the order of detention. The mere statement that the grounds do not disclose the grounds would not make a ground of vague. There may be a case where the grounds are irrelevant but the grounds are such that the order of the detaining authority is vitiated by any extraneous consideration. The grounds may be such as to prejudice the detenu. The grounds have been clearly vague and not such as to affect the constitutional right of the detenue to be furnished. The mere omission to disclose the grounds does not make the order of preventive detention illegal. The grounds do not contain any details of the grounds which are vague. There could be no doubt as to the nature of the grounds and the grounds. It is only the grounds which have been mentioned in the grounds. If the grounds are mentioned in the ground, the grounds would be vague. If the ground is vague, the grounds could not have been vague but the grounds could have been vague, and the grounds could, therefore, have been vaguely vague. The question whether the grounds were irrelevant or not was not a question of fact. The grounds, therefore, were vague.

The Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, was passed to provide for the better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make bye laws for the regulation of the business and the conditions of trading therein. The appellants were the owners of the notified agricultural crops in the state of Madras and were carrying on the business of selling and selling of agricultural crops in Madras. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the provisions of section 14 of the Act are not ultra vires the Act and they are not prohibited from holding the market as property, for they could still do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also do business outside the prescribed area. The appellants had not only two fundamental rights but also had a right to do business in their own market established subject of the Act. The appellants have not only two rights but also have a right to carry on business in the markets established subject to regulations and also to do business outside their respective areas. The appellants are not entitled to do business as a market committee. The appellants cannot, therefore, be said to have a right of appeal to the market committee. They are not prohibited by the Act or bye laws framed thereunder. They are entitled to do so. The appellants, therefore, cannot be said to be a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14. The appellants must be held to have a licence to trade in the market and the provisions of that section must be held not to be ultra vires the provisions of any of the Act or the bye laws framed under it. The appellants could not, therefore, claim that they were not entitled to the benefit of the Act as they were not prohibited from carrying on their business in the Market established subject to regulation and also do trade allowance. The appellants ' contention that the Act and Rules framed thereunder are ultra vires the State Legislature is rejected. The appellants therefore cannot be said, to have a fundamental right to carry out their business in a market established subject, to regulations and to do business within the prescribed area, and the provisions thereof are not ultra virus. The appellants can, therefore, not be said to possess a right of an appeal to the Market Committee. The appellants may, therefore, have a right under the Act to appeal to the Committee. The right to carry it out is a right which is not a right of a citizen to do business. The High court held that the appellants were not entitled under article 286(i)(b) to the benefit. The High 'Court further held that the sales were not sales within the meaning of article 286 (1)(b). The appellant then filed a writ appeal to the High Court.
